headline: AI-driven workforce disruption is creating acute financial vulnerability for executive women, requiring 6–12 month emergency cash buffers and proactive debt elimination
reasoning: Katrina Pulbrook notes that six executive women clients reached out in two weeks after redundancy, with roles in project work, administration and technical fields particularly exposed to AI displacement. She argues that high earners often take on proportionally large financial commitments (mortgages, personal loans, car leases, family obligations), meaning income loss is especially devastating. Her five-step preparedness framework centres on: building 6–12 months of emergency cash, auditing discretionary spending, eliminating non-deductible debt, seeking professional financial and accounting advice, and continuous upskilling. She emphasises that redundancy is not a personal failure but a structural workforce shift that will continue, and that having financial breathing room is critical to avoiding panic-driven decisions.
quote: The preparation is really in five steps. And the first one is, um, you know, basically what we want to do is make sure we've got an emergency cash buffer that's really, really important. So that's usually 6 to 12 months worth of your income that's sitting there that you can lean on for the future. The second one is making sure that you understand what all your commitments are, and these are not the regular ones such as mortgage, etc. these are more around the other expenses that we do on a day to day basis, where we might be a little bit more frivolous than most. The third one is making sure that we eliminate any unnecessary non deductible debt. And this is not just the mortgages because we've got to live somewhere. But there's also things personal loans, credit cards you know high leases on cars. Have a look at those and think in the dream of me not having a job, how would I cope with paying for all of these as well?
episode_title: The financial buffer for an AI-driven job loss | the advisory

headline: AI-driven workforce disruption is real but also creates opportunity; redundancy is not personal failure and individuals must build financial flexibility to avoid panic-selling investments
reasoning: Katrina Pulbrook argues that AI is creating both opportunities and disadvantages, particularly around workforce changes and redundancies. She emphasises that a high salary does not equate to wealth if outgoings are equally large, and that individuals must build financial flexibility. In the event of redundancy, people should avoid panic-selling investments or grabbing any available job, and instead treat the situation as a catalyst for reinvention — potentially through consulting, small business, or a career change. The ability to make deliberate choices rather than reactive ones requires prior financial preparation.
quote: What we've got to be aware of though, is that redundancies are not something that's a personal failure. It might feel that way, but it's absolutely not. It's about the changing workforce. But we need to be able to have that flexibility, to be able to use this as a catalyst and know that if you are a got a very big salary coming in the door, that doesn't make you rich, okay. Because of the commitments that you have going out, you have to create your own flexibility. And we also need to be aware that if if you do have a knock on the door and that redundancy package is happening, you've got a vast amount of experience, you have a lot of networks and the ability to be able to use that and also reinvent yourself and make some lifestyle choices and also be able to possibly start, you know, consulting or a small business or going into something completely different. You need to be able to create the choice when that happens, and not just grab any job that comes along because you have a panic and you don't start selling down investments too quickly.
episode_title: The financial buffer for an AI-driven job loss | the advisory
